How to submit music to radio stations in New York

By the RadioReach team Updated August 19, 2026 2 min read Country & market guides

On this page
  • Map the New York radio markets
  • Build the station-type layers
  • Use a truthful local angle
  • State campaign research workflow
  • What the pitch should contain
  • Measure market progress

New York State contains several different radio ecosystems. New York City is a global media market with intense competition, while the Hudson Valley, Capital Region, Central New York, Finger Lakes, Western New York, Long Island, and college towns create more regional programming paths.

Map the New York radio markets

Separate New York City from the rest of the state at the start; their contact density, local angles, and realistic first targets are different.

  • New York City: community, college, public, online, and specialty programs are more realistic than major commercial daytime rotation.
  • Long Island and Hudson Valley: local shows and tour context can distinguish a relevant pitch.
  • Albany, Syracuse, Ithaca, and college markets: campus/community schedules often create direct genre routes.
  • Rochester, Buffalo, and Western New York: distinct scenes, public/community outlets, colleges, and cross-border touring context.

Do not treat a state as one format. Separate markets, station types, and individual shows in your working list. A regional connection can improve a pitch, but only after the program actually fits the release.

Build the station-type layers

  1. College and community: find current music directors, genre directors, and local or specialty shows.
  2. Public and noncommercial: identify locally produced music blocks rather than pitching a network identity.
  3. Internet and syndicated shows: qualify active programming through recent episodes and tracklists.
  4. Commercial specialty: approach only where the format and current programming make the release plausible.

Upstate and regional targets should not be treated as overflow from an NYC campaign. Research their own venues, scenes, show schedules, and public playlists.

Use a truthful local angle

Name the borough, city, county, campus, collaborator, press outlet, or confirmed date that creates relevance. “New York artist” is too broad when the station serves a specific upstate community.

A local angle never substitutes for music fit. Check the show schedule and at least one recent playlist, then name the relevant signal in the first sentence. If you have no genuine tie, pitch a specialist on sound rather than manufacturing a geographic story.

State campaign research workflow

  1. Choose one focus track and define its narrow genre lane.
  2. List the markets connected to your home, audience, collaborators, press, or confirmed tour dates.
  3. Find specific shows in each market and record why each is a fit.
  4. Verify the current contact, official submission route, source URL, and date checked.
  5. Send in market-sized waves, beginning two to three weeks before release or a tour date.
  6. Follow up once, suppress opt-outs and bounces, and thank verified supporters.

What the pitch should contain

  • Artist, track, precise genre, and release date in the subject
  • The current presenter's name and one program-specific sentence
  • One stable stream with clean and downloadable versions available
  • A concise, verifiable New York connection where relevant
  • A direct request for consideration—never a claim that airplay is owed

For NYC specialists, lead with precise genre fit and evidence. For regional programs, combine that fit with a local or tour fact and make interview availability realistic for the station's time zone and format.

Measure market progress

Track qualified prospects, verified roles, sends, hard bounces, replies, adds, spins, interviews, and opt-outs separately. Save a public playlist or archive URL for every reported result. A campaign succeeds when it creates repeatable station relationships and credible evidence—not when it sends the largest number of emails.

Frequently asked questions

What radio stations should an independent artist target in New York?

Start with current college, community, public specialty, local-music, and internet programs. Match the city and show before moving toward highly centralized commercial playlists.

Do I need to live in New York to pitch its radio stations?

No. Genre shows can program national and international artists, while local showcases may define a borough, city, region, or state eligibility rule. Follow that rule exactly.

Is this a current list of stations accepting music?

No. This is a market-planning guide. Submission policies and staff change, so verify every station and contact on the outlet's official website before outreach.
